content:
In my opinion the Lean community is currently facing a problem:

There are many tasks which we see as important, but which do not get the credit they deserve.

For example making code "Mathlib ready", refactoring existing code to make it easier to use, helping new members on-board to Lean, reviewing code etc. I think this has been made worse with the advent of AI.

We are not the first or only academic community to face this problem. It has happened on large particle physics experiments for decades. There they have a solution - write papers with "3000 authors" in alphabetical order.

I know this has been mentioned on this Zulip before by others (sometimes in jest), but I think it is actually worth at least having a conversation about whether such a model would work for the Lean community.

Here is a quick summary of how I think the process would actually work (based on how it works for these experiments):

  • Joining would be completely optional.
  • To join you have to do a qualification project.
  • Once past the qualification project you are on all papers produced by the collaboration.
  • An internal record is kept of the actual main contributors to each paper, allowing people to claim as such on CVs etc.
  • After an extended period of inactivity, the person is removed from the collaboration.

What are peoples thoughts? Are there any obvious reasons why this wouldn't work here despite working for particle physics experiments? Are there perhaps downsides one should consider?
Do these papers get published? Who would publish such a lean paper?

Yeah - these papers get published all the time in ordinary journals within the field. It is standard practice, even smaller experiments take the same approach - I really think because it solves essentially the same problem I articulated above.

It is not so much different from the equational theories paper which has ~34 authors. I also don't see why the number of authors on a paper should matter here.

BTW, just in case there is confusion, I'm not saying we publish papers on making code "mathlib ready", the content of the papers will be as they are now.
I'm quite sure this would lead to yet much more low-to-medium-quality AI submissions. (An important difference with what CERN does is that those people are employed by CERN.)

@Adomas Baliuka I don't think I follow how this would lead to AI submissions? Also the comment about what CERN does isn't true, there are many people working on these CERN experiments throughout the world paid for by different institutions - very very few are paid directly by CERN.

Sorry, "employed" was sloppy. What I'm trying to say: I imagine all of those people are either directly part of CERN or employed/enrolled at research institutions/companies which have contracts or at least formal collaborations with CERN. The important point being that CERN can verify who those people are and very few people are trying to send someone AI-generated letters about grand unification hoping to get an authorship.

Agreed. But what would stop us also verifying who the people are, and in a sense controlling the qualification projects? In the CERN case you can't just send an AI-generated letter about grand-unification because that is not how the process works (not sure if I missed something here).

How do you verify the people? Do you set up a network of universities/companies/organizations and only accept their official collaborators/students/employees? Only accept collaborators who participated (and maybe submitted a paper on their "qualification project") in some conference/event (and paid a fee)? Or could anyone on Zulip in principle try to do such a "qualification project"?

It's very unclear what "qualification project" means. If it's something that just anyone can try to do (which might seem ideal from the spirit of Mathlib, where right now it's still possible to contribute basically anonymously), I expect those projects will be swamped with AI submissions.

In the CERN case the projects tend to be the sort of things which are really important but wouldn't necessarily lead to publication. I can imagine in the Lean case it would be "refractor ...". They are also not something someone can do in an afternoon - they are months long projects (basically equivalent to the amount of work needed to write a paper).

In terms of verifying people, I think the idea would be that after the qualification project, there is a pretty good idea how good they are, and if they are serious or not. (One could also build in a collaborative aspect to it).
Here is a doc on qualification tasks at ATLAS (one of the CERN experiments)

What I personally dislike of this idea is that it's not trying to disrupt the publish-or-perish model, rather embracing it. If we agree that treating publications and papers as the strongest available currency is flawed because it doesn't recognise crucial contributions, the answer should be "value those contributions!", not to turn them into papers. This is hard, takes time an requires a mental shift, yet I would suggest we try it.

@Filippo A. E. Nuccio I think this is a fair criticism. The problem is that publications and citations, are the common currency that academia, grant bodies etc., works with. It is in a sense the universal quantifiable measure by which people across disciplines can be compared (rightly or wrongly).

The only way I can see a system without papers working is if we come up with a way to quantify contributions, and a way to translate those contributions into something which can be compared with directly with papers and citations.

No doubt there is a precedence for this somewhere. I think such a system would be fairly easy to implement.

  • Make a website akin to that of a journal.
  • Allow people to submit their contributions to said website (consisting of a title, the authors, a short description, the relevant github PRs, and links to other contributions this depends on).
  • Send it out for review (probably a light form of review for things in e.g. mathlib)
  • Package all this together on a webpage with a doi.
  • have on the webpage a statement about the correspondence between contributions and papers.

Well, on a one hand having contributed to founding the I'm certainly not in favour of a system "without papers", just to put them back where they belonged, namely in the category of vehicles carrying and disseminating scientific advances rather than in a stock exchange. And for your second point, Mathlib is already basically what you describe: if you're missing the DOI part, commits could be a good proxy and permanent Software Heritage id's are almost verbatim the same as DOIs.

Kevin Buzzard said:

Do these papers get published?

Here's one on the arXiv from yesterday https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.05512 submitted, it says, to Physics Review Letters. Here's a relatively recent one that's published in Physics Review D https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01219, the authors are listed after the references.

From the slides Joseph shared:

A TRT qualification task is defined such that it constitutes important work that
fits within the one-year qualification period

qualification is nontrivial, perhaps more demanding than what currently seems to be the case (to me an outsider) for people to contribute a single PR to Mathlib, but maybe getting a few "real-sized" PRs accepted and merged to Mathlib, as well as some contribution to PR reviews is comparable.
I also think that the qualification task are approved beforehand (there might even be a list somewhere) - i.e. people know what they have to do before they start, it is not a mystery.

Just had a conversation with @Sven Krippendorf , who mentioned Euclid has a different type of authorship policy to some of the CERN experiments. It's detailed here:

https://www.euclid-ec.org/science/publications/
I personally really like the idea. Asking that academia changes the way it evaluates everyones contributions is great in principle but is not very practical. This seems like a great compromise.

@Brian Nugent you mean the CERN-style collaboration idea? If so I think the main obstacle from doing this, is that I think for it to work, we would need some non-trivial critical mass of people to join from the start.
Yeah, there’s also the issue of who would run such a thing. But I like the idea!

Filippo A. E. Nuccio said:

Well, on a one hand having contributed to found the I'm certainly not in favour of a system "without papers", just to put them back where they belonged, namely in the category of vehicles carrying and disseminating scientific advances rather than in a stock exchange. And for your second point, Mathlib is already basically what you describe: of you're missing the DOI part, commits could be a good proxy and permanent Software Heritage id's are almost verbatim the same as DOIs.

This is a different conversation topic, so should likely be moved to a different thread. I think the problem with commits is that they are too fine-grained, you could not link to them on a CV for example. But I think even a simple website where people can package together pull-requests, write a small description, and give it a title would help here (and should be fairly easy to put together). Not to replace papers, but to catalog, and reference contributions. What I have in mind is something like the attached (AI-generated) image.

I'm new to the Lean community and my exposure has been limited to PhysLib so far, but I'm familiar with the high-energy collaborations. I've been thinking about this for a while and I'd like to share some thoughts. The punchline is that I don't see how any of the existing systems, in their current incarnation, can help the community thrive. There are aspects of existing systems which we can take, but I think we should re-think much of the system itself. In that sense, the credit issue @Joseph Tooby-Smith raised is one symptom of a bigger issue. The CERN model is clever because it obviously offers an advantage to the people in the community over other communities but, much like what @Filippo A. E. Nuccio was saying, it accepts a premise I don't like.

The publication system is about to break down — arXiv in March 2026 had a record ~30k submissions, reviewers are impossible to find, and AI is making it worse by flooding the pipeline with plausible but low-signal content. This is happening in several disciplines, and no community can ignore it. I think the problem is the concept of the scientific paper itself, as the main mean of sharing knowledge among experts. This is a discussion in and of itself and I want to remain on point so I'm not adding more on this here. My point is: I don't think any system based on the current concept of a scientific paper can work.

At the same time there are obvious private interests investing in Lean — AI labs are training on Mathlib, startups are building verification tools. That's good: it means the community is building something valuable. But it also means the window for the community to set its own terms will likely narrow because of outside interests. The point I want to make is that the industry of Scientific publishing is a cautionary tale: researchers produce the content, review for free, and then pay to read their own work, because the academic community did not build a good infrastructure. We should avoid this

Instead of adapting the paper to fit our workflow, we should adapt the credit system (I think we need one) to fit the actual workflow, based on pull requests. A PR goes through CI, linters, style checks, maintainer review, and rounds of revision before merge — it's already a more honest record of contribution than any paper. We can treat the merged PR as the unit of contribution (we can think of standardizing that). Credit flows backward through the dependency tree (imports, declarations used), weighted by distance. Reviewers appear in the record too. Refactorers get credit alongside the original author — to avoid the perverse incentive of avoiding cleanup work. In that sense, the paper doesn't disappear; you can still write one for narrative and context. But the contribution lives in the repository, and the paper becomes commentary. I agree with @Filippo A. E. Nuccio point about Software Heritage IDs basically functioning as DOIs — we're mostly there in terms of existence of tools. What's missing is the layer that packages PRs into something legible to hiring committees or grant panels.

Now, whatever system we end up creating, at scale it will have to confront the problem that more people want to create, less want to review. If we assign PRs based on skills proven by previous work, you can try and balance the number of PRs that an individual can submit with the number of PR that an individual should check.

I want to bring an issue of sustainability. The libraries should be stewarded by a community-related body — that's the trust layer. It feels like this is happening in Mathlib but I don't know enough. A company or companies can build valuable products on top (managed verification pipelines, AI tools trained on the corpus, consulting) as long as the community has an explicit stake and the principles are made clear. There are stories of open-source companies like Red Hat, Databricks, and Redis that offer ideas and things to be wary of.

I'm writing a longer version of all this for myself. If people are interested, I can put it as a living document, open for comments and edits.

Funny timing — I came here mostly looking for Lean / mathlib metatheory discussions, and then I stumbled onto this thread.

A lot of what you’re describing is very close to something I’ve been formalizing from a different angle in EpArchhttps://github.com/loumaloulongtin/EpArch/tree/grounded-spec.

In the framework, this kind of overload problem is basically an epistemic DDoS: too much plausible-looking content hitting a validation surface with limited review capacity.

What I found especially interesting is that your proposed response aligns closely with the mechanism set my formalization derives under those kinds of pressures: a shared authorization layer / ledger, explicit provenance and dependency metadata, scoped trust / governance, and structured review paths instead of pretending everything can be revalidated from scratch each time.

The one part I think still needs to be made more explicit is the correction layer: not just how to assign credit and route trust, but how to handle the things that still get through anyway — quarantine, rollback, supersession, that kind of thing.

By the way, one small structural thought: before we get to this paragraph, the post can read a bit like an anti-paper argument:

I want to bring an issue of sustainability. The libraries should be stewarded by a community-related body — that's the trust layer. It feels like this is happening in Mathlib but I don't know enough. A company or companies can build valuable products on top (managed verification pipelines, AI tools trained on the corpus, consulting) as long as the community has an explicit stake and the principles are made clear. There are stories of open-source companies like Red Hat, Databricks, and Redis that offer ideas and things to be wary of.

I think this is actually the paragraph that really sets the table for the people you most want to reach. That’s the point where it becomes clear this isn’t just “papers are broken,” but “this ecosystem is becoming valuable, outside interests are real, and the community needs its own trust / governance layer before someone else defines the terms.” So even though it sounds a bit like a conclusion right now, I think moving this part earlier would make the whole post land even better.

@Fabio Anzà Thank you for your valuable contributions to the discussion. I would be very happy to get access to the longer form of the document, please feel free to reach out in DM (or publicly here, as you see fit).

Filippo A. E. Nuccio said:

... put them [papers] back where they belonged, namely in the category of vehicles carrying and disseminating scientific advances ... Mathlib is already basically what you describe: if you're missing the DOI part, commits could be a good proxy and permanent Software Heritage id's are almost verbatim the same as DOIs.

In the "category of vehicles carrying and disseminating scientific advances", if some folks are interested in the technological possibilities of DOI-like permanent IDs built on top of Git commits and Software Heritage, I have been experimenting with this. If interested, here are some links for more info:

  • Python package of the underling "document succession" tech: Hidos
  • a "paper" of the Document Succession Identifier specification: perm.pub/1wFGhvmv8XZfPx0O5Hya2e9AyXo
  • try.perm.pub is a particular incarnation of using Document Sucession Identifiers with a paper format based on what journals use (JATS XML)

If you opt to view that "paper" above on lens.perm.pub you are literally pulling the data directly from Software Heritage into your web browser session, the Git records are cryptographically checked, and then it's rendered on-the-fly into HTML from the "paper" format.

I'm new to Lean so I have not yet seen how this tech might be useful to the Lean community but I think there might be some bits and piece that might be useful for something. I have discovered many issues and problems with what I have developed.

I'm sorry to say this tech does not solve for the credit problem. It is in the "category of vehicles carrying and disseminating scientific advances". I am sceptical that any tech alone will solve the credit problem, which is more of a social and organizational problem.

That's awesome @Lou ! I just skimmed the repo and it indeed looks very very close to what I was describing. Thank you for this. I'll have to check it out properly

Lou said:

A lot of what you’re describing is very close to something I’ve been formalizing from a different angle in EpArchhttps://github.com/loumaloulongtin/EpArch/tree/grounded-spec.

In the framework, this kind of overload problem is basically an epistemic DDoS: too much plausible-looking content hitting a validation surface with limited review capacity.

I love the "epistemic DDoS" characterization. Never thought of it that way but its 100% that

The one part I think still needs to be made more explicit is the correction layer: not just how to assign credit and route trust, but how to handle the things that still get through anyway — quarantine, rollback, supersession, that kind of thing.

I agreed 100%. Using an error correction analogy – I think it's pointless to build a system which filters out all kinds of errors because the environment is too noisy. We have to build a robust correction layer: one that removes errors at a rate that is higher than the ones the environment puts in.

I think this is actually the paragraph that really sets the table for the people you most want to reach. That’s the point where it becomes clear this isn’t just “papers are broken,” but “this ecosystem is becoming valuable, outside interests are real, and the community needs its own trust / governance layer before someone else defines the terms.” So even though it sounds a bit like a conclusion right now, I think moving this part earlier would make the whole post land even better.

Thank you for pointing it out. Yes, it does read like a conclusion while it should really be a starting point. I'll take this into account in the document I'm writing. The reason for keeping together the thread "papers are broken" and "self governance of Mathlib/Physlib/ and other lean-based libraries" is that scientific publishing with "one paper as one unit" is both a cautionary tale on the self-governance element but also a broken assumption that we should probably move past.

I also really like what you @Castedo Ellerman are saying here

Castedo Ellerman said:

If you opt to view that "paper" above on lens.perm.pub you are literally pulling the data directly from Software Heritage into your web browser session, the Git records are cryptographically checked, and then it's rendered on-the-fly into HTML from the "paper" format.

I'm new to Lean so I have not yet seen how this tech might be useful to the Lean community but I think there might be some bits and piece that might be useful for something. I have discovered many issues and problems with what I have developed.

Specifically, this package could help in addressing one element of the "papers are broken" that has always bothered me: the fact that when we produce one piece of knowledge/science and put it in a paper, everyone reads the same content (it's a PDF-based paper) irrespectively of their previous knowledge. Having a lean-based asset that contains scientific knowledge paired with a translation layer that turns lean code into human-readable language would allow two things to happen at the same time. First you can search, import and re-use previous results while you work on developing new results. We partially have this already with things like leansearch.net; Second, while you work on staying updated, you can talk to a model that can interpret the Lean code and somehow fine-tune the level and specific type of context the model can use to interpret the code. This can be used as a powerful teaching and self-learning tool

I also 100% agree on this :point_down:

I'm sorry to say this tech does not solve for the credit problem. It is in the "category of vehicles carrying and disseminating scientific advances". I am sceptical that any tech alone will solve the credit problem, which is more of a social and organizational problem.

To be explicit: I agree that the tech alone won't solve this because of the social/organization aspects. However, the way I think about this is more informed by behavioral economic thinking. I'm asking myself (and people here) something like this. Assuming scientists want to balance private life and work (need to pay the bills and have valuable time outside the job) to an arbitrary degree (some people might choose 90% work while others will choose differently), how do we pair the sheer technological solution with the self-governance in a way that aligns the needs of the individual with the broader needs of the community? I don't have a complete answer yet but I think we can find one that is better than the current "grant and hiring committee systems".

Let me say, I fully agree with the general premise of crediting contributions, and not necessarily translating them into something like a paper.

However, I feel I am currently stuck on this point:

Fabio Anzà said:

A PR goes through CI, linters, style checks, maintainer review, and rounds of revision before merge — it's already a more honest record of contribution than any paper. We can treat the merged PR as the unit of contribution (we can think of standardizing that). Credit flows backward through the dependency tree (imports, declarations used), weighted by distance. Reviewers appear in the record too.

To me, I (currently) think that the PR is too small a unit of contribution. In particular, to me a unit of contribution of person X to Mathlib should contain information like:

  • X refactored category theory to make it easier to use.

Not something like:

  • X changed the name of Y to Z in Mathlib.

The latter is similar to the scale of a contribution of a PR, whilst the former is at a different scale (many 10s of PRs in some cases).

The former tells me very quickly what X has done, and it something that X could put on their CV or website, or tell current and future employers.

Is there a part of the above that addresses this?
I also don't see how to make the "credit flows backwards" work in practice.
Maybe what I am looking for is project Milestones on GitHub, as an example, I made one here for bumps of Physlib.
(Maybe this example is closer to what I have in mind as what should be a contribution unit.)

I think a related question to all of this is: Do we want a credit system that is based on a metric (e.g. something akin to a citation count, or a h-index), or something where credit is given based on actual review of contribution (as I believe things like REF in the UK try and do)? To me the latter is preferable, as long as we can disseminate contribution in a good way.
The "Impactstory" project might be a source of ideas (but not exactly what you want) ... here is an example profile https://profiles.impactstory.org/u/0000-0001-6728-7745

However, I caution to not create yet another example of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodhart%27s_law

When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure
GitHub has a very rich and extensive API ... so it can be used to create some kind of credit accounting summary that might be more familiar to academic audiences
perhaps maybe even output a Lean proof for a proposition corresponding to "you should fund/hire/promote me" :wink:

Another source of ideas might be from people trying to incentivize scientific data-sharing which is in some ways similar to this situation with Lean contributions e.g. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8796038/

Another tech worth being aware of is https://rogue-scholar.org/ because if you generate something that is like a blogsite where each blog post is some unit of credit that you like, then Rogue Scholar will make a DOI for that post ... it works with a large number of blog platforms

GitHub PRs don’t reflect anything. One person might make many PRs and another person might make fewer PRs. Some people might be mentoring others and so only filling out parts of proofs or even less on their own. You also have to ensure that coauthor commit messages are used.

Any fully automated credit accounting based on only GitHub PRs will result in a bad case of Goodhart's law. I'd wager anything trying to create a "unit" of credit is going to result in a case of Goodhart's law. But I can sympathize with the effort to find one for pragmatic reasons.

Once any form of credit accounting becomes tied to real consequences (hiring, funding, status), doesn’t it inevitably trigger Goodhart’s Law no matter how sophisticated the metric is? Curious if people have thoughts on escaping the credit frame entirely instead of optimizing inside it.

Escaping the credit frame, huh?

Would it mean no academic jobs, no research grants, only bounties on proving theorems?

Yes, that’s probably what it means. I wasn’t trying to push that as some kind of good idea.

My real point is: as long as there are social incentives (jobs, grants, status) attached to any measurable credit proxy, people will be incentivised to game it — the current paper system with paper mills already shows the issue. So the question is whether removing the credit ledger entirely is an acceptable way around Goodhart’s Law, or if there’s actually a “good” implementation versus a bad one. Curious what people think.

I don't have a real opinion here.

Lou said:

Once any form of credit accounting becomes tied to real consequences (hiring, funding, status), doesn’t it inevitably trigger Goodhart’s Law no matter how sophisticated the metric is?

I'd say this depends on how "good" does the "good" in Goodhart's law need to be to not "cease". In the realm of business the term "generally accepted" is used instead of "good" for example: GAAP in the US, Generally Accepted Accounting Principles https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accounting_standard
I see value in having something like GAAP in part because it actually evolves and changes as society collective changes opinion on what is or is not "good" enough as an imperfect accounting practice
Because people with money trying to decide where to put that money have limited time there must be some imperfect system because humans brains (with money in hand) are not perfect

I think my example of REF (research excellence framework) in the UK above is a case where they have tried to move away from a some sort of metric. In particular, I believe they decide the quality of a paper by sending it out to reviewers to read, who come back with some quantification of the quality (not entirely sure of the details here - sorry).

But I think a premise like this could hold here. We package contributions up into easy to digest, easy to read, easy to understand units, and then let hiring committees, grant panels etc. look at these contributions and make their own mind up about them. We can't expect these people to read 70 page long papers, but I think we can expect them to read abstract-length summaries.

I think whatever system is landed on (and I believe/hope we eventually will make such a change), then I think it is important that it cross-compatible with papers. In other words able to cite papers, and able to be cited by papers.
